transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Morning, come on in, have a seat. So... what brings you in today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Uh, morning. It's my back. Probably nothing, honestly, my wife just made me come.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Well, let's have a look anyway. How long has it been bothering you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Since, um... Saturday. Yeah, Saturday. We moved flats and I was carrying boxes up three flights of stairs, and on the last flight something sort of pulled.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: So about four days now. Where exactly is the pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Low down, on the right side. Just above the belt, more or less.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Does it travel anywhere? Down into your buttock or your leg?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, no. It just sits there. Well... it catches sometimes when I turn, but it doesn't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Any numbness or pins and needles in your legs, or around your groin?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And your waterworks and bowels, all normal? No trouble passing urine, no accidents?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ha, no. All normal.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Good. Any fever, or weight loss you can't explain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No fever. Weight's the same. If anything I've put some on, my wife says.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: On a scale where zero is nothing and ten is the worst pain imaginable, how bad is it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Um... a six? When I bend down to put my socks on it's more like a seven. Sitting's fine, I drive a delivery van so I'm sitting all day, but climbing out of the van, uh, that's a bit sharp.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: What have you taken for it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A couple of paracetamol on Sunday, and one ibuprofen yesterday, I think. Didn't really notice much difference.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Have you had back trouble before?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Once. Years ago, maybe ten? It went away by itself.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Okay. Can you stand up for me and bend forward as far as you can... mm-hm, and come back up. Now hop on the couch and lie on your back. I'm going to lift this leg. Any pain going down the leg?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just a pull in my back. Not down the leg.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Other side. Okay. Now push against my hand... and the other one. Good, equal strength. Knee reflexes are normal too.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Right, so the muscles on the right side of your lower back are tender and tight, and you're a bit stiff bending forward, but the nerve tests are all normal. This fits with a strained muscle, what we call mechanical back pain.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So it's not a disc or something? My brother had a slipped disc and he was in bed for weeks.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Nothing here points to that. No leg symptoms, no tingling, normal strength. And honestly, bed rest is the worst thing for this. Staying moving is better.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. So what do I take? The paracetamol didn't do much.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'd go with ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, three times a day, always with food, for up to a week. You can add paracetamol, up to a thousand milligrams four times a day, if it's still sore. A warm pad on the back can help too.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I need a sick note? I mean, I can probably still drive...

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Not necessarily. Keep working if you can manage, just avoid heavy lifting for a bit. If you find you can't do the job, call me. And come back right away if you get numbness, weakness in a leg, or any problem with your bladder or bowels. Otherwise, if it isn't clearly better in two weeks, come and see me again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Alright. Thanks, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Hi, come in, sit down. What can I do for you today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hi. Um, so, this is a bit embarrassing, but I think I've got a bladder infection? Again.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: That's nothing to be embarrassed about, it's really common. Tell me what's been happening.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It started last night. A burning feeling when I pee, and I need to go all the time, like every twenty minutes, and then only a tiny bit comes out.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Okay. Any blood in the urine?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hmm... this morning it looked a bit pink? Maybe. I'm not sure, I had beetroot salad yesterday so it could just be that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Fair enough, we'll check that. Any fever or shivering? Pain in your sides or your back?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No fever, I feel fine otherwise. There's a dull ache low down in my tummy, but not in my back. A friend of mine had kidney stones and she said it started in the back, so I was a bit worried at first.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Pain low in the tummy fits with the bladder. Any discharge or itching down below?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And is there any chance you could be pregnant?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No... well, my period's due in about three days, but I'm on the pill and I take it properly, so no.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Okay. You said 'again'. When was the last infection?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Uh, about eight months ago? Maybe seven. I got antibiotics from, um, another doctor, one covering for you I think. A short course, and it worked.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Do you remember which antibiotic?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Nitro... something? Little capsules.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Probably nitrofurantoin. Any allergies to medication?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, none.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Good. Let me feel your tummy. Tell me if anything hurts... here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ow, yeah, a bit. Just above the bone.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Mild tenderness just above the pubic bone. And I'll tap on your back, either side... no pain there? Good. Your temperature is 36.9, so no fever. And you brought a urine sample, thanks. The dipstick shows nitrite positive, white cells two plus, and a trace of blood.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So it is an infection.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Yes, a straightforward bladder infection, cystitis. Nothing to suggest the kidneys are involved. I'll prescribe nitrofurantoin, 100 milligrams modified release, twice a day for five days, with food.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Should I stop drinking coffee or something?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You don't have to, but drink plenty of water. Paracetamol is fine for the discomfort. If you get a fever, pain in your back, or you start vomiting, or if it hasn't improved in two to three days, call us straight away. And if these infections keep coming back, we'll think about looking into it further.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Great, thank you so much.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Take a seat. This is your blood pressure review, correct?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, yes. Uh, I brought my notebook. My daughter said I should write the numbers down, so I did. Most days.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Excellent. What have the readings been?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Let me find... um, here. Mostly one-forty-something over eighty-something. The highest was one fifty-eight over ninety-two, but that was after the neighbours' barbecue, so, you know, salty sausages.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Understood. Are you taking the amlodipine every day, five milligrams?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Mostly. Well... two or three days a week I forget. The mornings are chaos, I've got the dog, he's a labrador, and he's got this thing where he, uh, he won't go out unless...

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Let's keep to the point. Could you leave the tablet next to your toothbrush?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, that's a good idea, actually.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Any side effects? Headaches, dizziness?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No dizziness. But my ankles swell up by the evening. My socks leave marks. I thought it was just age. It started, hm, maybe a month or two after I began the tablets? So spring, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Any chest pain or breathlessness?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, no. I walk the dog for an hour every day, no trouble at all.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Do you smoke? And how much do you drink?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stopped smoking in 2009. Alcohol, a couple of beers at the weekend. Maybe three on Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: All right. Let me take your pressure. ... It's 152 over 94, pulse 72 and regular. Let me look at your ankles. Yes, mild pitting swelling on both sides. Heart sounds are normal and the lungs are clear.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that bad? The numbers?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's above where we want it. And the ankle swelling is most likely a side effect of the amlodipine. So I'd like to stop it and switch you to lisinopril, 10 milligrams once daily, in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Can I finish the amlodipine box first? I've got half a box left.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: No, stop it and start the lisinopril tomorrow. I'd like a blood test in one to two weeks to check your kidney function and potassium. Some people get a dry cough with lisinopril, so let me know if that happens.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Right. And the diary, keep going with that?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Yes please, keep writing the numbers down. Cut back on salt where you can. Bring the diary and we'll recheck in four weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Toothbrush. Got it.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Hello, hi there. And who do we have here?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: This is Noah, he's four. Um, he's had this cough for about five days now, and last night was really bad, I barely slept, and he was making this, uh, whistling sound when he breathed.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: A whistling sound. Was that when he was breathing in or out?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Out, I think? It's hard to tell... yeah, out. Mostly when he was lying down.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Okay. Has he had a fever?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: The first day, yes. Thirty-eight, maybe thirty-eight point two, I gave him paracetamol and it went away. Nothing since Sunday.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Is he eating and drinking?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Drinking, yes. Eating not so much, but he's picky anyway. He did have yoghurt and half a banana this morning.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And is he peeing normally?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Yes, yes, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Is he bringing anything up when he coughs? Phlegm?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: It sounds wet. Sometimes he gags a bit. No blood or anything like that.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Has he had wheezing before? Asthma, eczema?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Um... he had bronchiolitis when he was one, in the winter, but that's it. And a bit of eczema as a baby.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Does he go to daycare? Anyone else unwell?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Three days a week. Half the group has been coughing, honestly.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Any smoking in the house?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: No, no.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And his vaccinations are up to date?

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Yes, all done.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Great. Noah, can I listen to your chest? Big breaths for me, like a dragon...

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: He's a bit shy. Come on, sweetheart.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: That's fine, he's doing well. Temperature is 36.8. Breathing rate 28 a minute, which is fine for his age. Oxygen level 97 percent. Throat's a little red, ears look normal. In the chest, there's some wheeze when he breathes out, both sides, but no crackles, and he's not working hard to breathe, no pulling in at the ribs.

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: So what is it?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: This looks like a viral chest infection with some mild wheezing. No sign of pneumonia.

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Oh. My neighbour said he'd definitely need antibiotics.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Antibiotics only work on bacteria, and this is a virus, so they wouldn't help. What I'd do is give him a salbutamol inhaler with a spacer, two puffs up to every four hours when he's wheezy or coughing a lot. I'll show you how to use it. Keep him drinking, and paracetamol if he's uncomfortable, dose on the packet according to his weight.

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: And when can he go back to daycare?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Once he's fever-free and breathing comfortably. Come back or call if he's breathing fast or struggling, if you see his ribs pulling in, if he won't drink, or if the fever comes back. And if he's still wheezy in a week, bring him in again.

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: Okay, thank you, that's a relief.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Hi, come in. How are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Honestly? Tired. Um, that's why I'm here, really. I've been exhausted for about two months and I thought it would pass, but it hasn't.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Two months. Is it there all day, or at certain times?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: All day. I wake up and I'm already tired. By three in the afternoon I could just... fall asleep at my desk. I started a new job in September too, so I thought, you know, it's the stress. But...

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: How's your sleep?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not great. I fall asleep fine, but I wake up around four and then I'm just lying there thinking about emails. Maybe six hours a night, in total.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Does anyone notice snoring, or you stopping breathing at night?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ha, my husband says I snore sometimes, but nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Okay. Any weight change, fevers, night sweats?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No... well, I haven't weighed myself. My jeans fit the same.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: What about appetite and diet?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Appetite's fine. I'm mostly vegetarian, though. I eat fish sometimes.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And your periods, how are they?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Heavy. They've been heavy for a while, like a year. The first three days I change something every two or three hours. Regular though, every twenty-eight days.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Any shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness when you stand up?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit breathless on the stairs at work, I noticed that. No palpitations. No dizziness, really.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Have you been feeling low in mood, or lost interest in things?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Um... a bit flat, maybe, but I think that's just because I'm tired. I still enjoy things. I saw friends on Saturday and had a lovely time.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Are you on any medication or supplements?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Nothing. Occasionally an ibuprofen for period pain.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Let me check a few things. Blood pressure is 118 over 74, pulse 72 and regular. Your eyelids look a bit pale on the inside. Thyroid isn't enlarged. Heart and lungs sound normal, and your tummy is soft and not tender.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what do you think it is?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It could be several things, and probably a mix. Heavy periods and a mostly vegetarian diet make me think of low iron. We should also check your thyroid, vitamin B12 and blood sugar. The poor sleep and the new job are probably contributing as well.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Should I just buy iron pills in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I'd wait for the results first. I'll order a full blood count, ferritin, TSH, B12 and glucose. I'll phone you with the results in three or four days. In the meantime, try a regular sleep schedule, screens off an hour before bed, and no caffeine after noon. Let's see each other again in two weeks to go through everything and talk about the heavy periods.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Thank you, that's a relief, I thought it was all in my head.
